paras: The lynching of Lemmel Walters was the killing of a 17-year-old Black man in Longview, Texas, who was taken from the town jail by a crowd of white men and shot on or shortly before July 4, 1919. No charge had been made against him, and the only cause the report gave was a white woman's statement that she loved him. The Chicago Defender reported the killing under a headline accusing local police of trying to keep it secret.

According to a Defender dispatch datelined Longview, July 4, a "prominent white woman" had told her personal friends that she loved Walters and that if she were in the North she would get a divorce and marry him. Walters was arrested at Glore, Texas, and then moved to the Longview jail, which the dispatch called being "spirited here for 'safe living.'" The Defender stated that "no charge was preferred against Walters other than the statement made by the white woman to her personal friends."

A crowd of white men came to the Longview jail and seized Walters. A garbled passage in the printed text appears to say that someone at the jail welcomed the mob and greeted the men as they passed through the gate, but it does not make clear who. The men took Walters to the outskirts of town and "shot [him] to pieces," then threw his body near the roadside. He was buried by Black people of the area.

According to the Defender, officials made every effort to keep the outside world from learning of the lynching, but the news leaked out. The woman was said to be "prostrated" and under a physician's care at Glore. The dispatch reported that white people were angry because Black residents had been leaving that part of Texas "in droves," and that all the farm hands had left since the lynching. No report of an inquest, an arrest or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The only Black-press report found was a short item on page 2 of the Chicago Defender of July 5, 1919, headed "Police Work to Keep Lynching a Secret." The Defender's account centered on official concealment and the lack of any charge, and it presented the killing as the result of a white woman's affection rather than any act by Walters. It closed by tying the lynching to the movement of Black workers out of that part of Texas.

reader.title: Lynching of Lemmel Walters
bases: A crowd of white men took Walters from the Longview jail and shot him to death outside town, and the Defender called the killing a lynching [A1].

Per the Chicago Defender, a "crowd of white men" seized Walters from jail without any charge and shot him "to pieces" because a white woman had said she loved him, a racial offense under the standard definition [A1]. The account rests on a single Black-press dispatch [A1].
Only one report, the Chicago Defender's Longview dispatch, was found in the Black press [A1].
